[[4:19|Jason sent|Misit Jason]] men [[4:19|to carry three hundred didrachmas of silver for the sacrifice of Hercules|portantes argenti didrachmas trecentas in sacrificium Herculis]]: [[4:19|but the bearers thereof desired|quas postulaverunt hi qui asportaverunt]], that is, those who took it with them, [[4:19|it might not be bestowed on the sacrifices|ne in sacrificiis Herculis erogarentur]] of Hercules, [[4:19|because it was not necessary|quia non oporteret]], that is, it was neither needful, nor indeed useful. But, [[4:20|because of them that carried it|Propter præsentes autem]], that is, at the instance of those who were there, it [[4:20|was employed for the making of galleys|datæ sunt in fabricam navium triremium]], that is, for building ships in which there were three banks of oars.

paras.t: Misso autem in Ægyptum Apollonio, quem illuc misit Antiochus propter primates Ptolemæi Philometoris regis Ægypti, cujus aliqua oppida occupavit Antiochus: quæ primates præfati Ptolemæi adhuc adolescentuli, requirebant ab Antiocho; principes Ptolemæi contra eum, oppida illa reddere non volentem, pugnam moverunt. Quum cognovisset Antiochus alienum se a negotiis regni Ægypti effectum, venit Jerosolymam. Fuit enim ab Ægypto per Romanorum legatos repulsus, ut dictum est plenius in expositione primi libri. Et magnifice a Jasone, quem ad pontificatum simoniace ac perverse promovit, et civitate susceptus, cum facularum luminibus et laudibus ingressus est; et inde in Phœnicen exercitum convertit. Verumtamen tunc, ut videtur, fecit mala multa et magna, quæ primi libri capitulo primo recitantur.
paras.en: [[4:21|Now when Apollonius, the son of Mnestheus was sent into Egypt|Misso autem in Ægyptum Apollonio]], whom Antiochus sent there [[4:21|to treat with the nobles of king Philometor|propter primates Ptolemæi Philometoris regis Ægypti]], some of whose towns Antiochus had seized (towns which the nobles of the aforesaid Ptolemee, still a youth, were demanding back from Antiochus; and Ptolemee's princes made war on him when he would not give those towns back): when [[4:21|Antiochus understood that he was wholly excluded from the affairs of the kingdom|cognovisset Antiochus alienum se a negotiis regni Ægypti effectum]] of Egypt, he came [[4:21|to Jerusalem|venit Jerosolymam]]. For he was driven back from Egypt by the envoys of the Romans, as was said more fully in the exposition of the first book. [[4:22|Where he was received in a magnificent manner by Jason|Et magnifice a Jasone]], whom he had promoted to the high priesthood simoniacally and perversely, [[4:22|and the city|et civitate susceptus]], [[4:22|and came in with torch lights, and with praises|cum facularum luminibus et laudibus ingressus est]], [[4:22|and from thence he returned with his army into Phenicia|et inde in Phœnicen exercitum convertit]]. Yet at that time, it seems, he did many great evils, which are related in the first chapter of the first book[[1 Mach 1:22||]].

paras.t: Et post triennii tempus misit Jason frater Oniæ, Menelaum, supradicti Simonis fratrem, portantem pecunias regi Antiocho, et de negotiis necessariis, id est de causis sibi commissis, responsa perlaturum, id est reportaturum a rege. Circa hæc incidit quæstio, quomodo Menelaus iste dicatur frater Simonis supradicti, qui (ut præcedenti fertur capitulo) de Benjamin fuit tribu; Jason autem et Onias de tribu Levi et Aaron erant. Josephus autem apertissime scribit duodecimo Antiquitatum libro, quod Jason et Menelaus fuerunt fratres Oniæ. Hinc Lyra hoc loco negat Josephum, propter hujus libri auctoritatem. Verum Magister in historiis et alii multi authentici et antiqui Catholici, secuti sunt Josephum: et rationabiliter, ut videtur. Judæi enim non sustinuissent Menelaum in pontificatu, nisi de genere Aaron exstitisset. Nec post reditum a Babylonica captivitate leguntur Judæi unquam aliquem habuisse pontificem, nisi de stirpe Levi et Aaron. Quod autem Menelaus dicitur fuisse frater Simonis supradicti, quidam exponunt dicentes, quod fuit frater ejus non carnis propagatione, sed imitatione et conformitate malitiæ. Juxta quem modum in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Qui effundit sanguinem, et qui fraudem facit mercenario, fratres sunt. Posset etiam dici, quod quia tribus Levi poterat cum ceteris tribubus Israel matrimonia sociare, Menelaus iste ex parte unius parentis, præsertim matris, forsitan fuit de Benjamin tribu et Simonis frater.
paras.en: [[4:23|Three years afterwards Jason sent|Et post triennii tempus misit Jason]], the brother of Onias, [[4:23|Menelaus, brother of the aforesaid Simon|Menelaum, supradicti Simonis fratrem]], [[4:23|to carry money to the king|portantem pecunias regi]] Antiochus, and, [[4:23|concerning certain necessary affairs|et de negotiis necessariis]], that is, the matters committed to him, [[4:23|to bring answers from him|responsa perlaturum]], that is, to carry them back from the king. Here a question arises: how this Menelaus can be called the brother of the aforesaid Simon, who (as is told in the preceding chapter) was of the tribe of Benjamin[[2 Mach 3:4||]], whereas Jason and Onias were of the tribe of Levi and of Aaron. Josephus, indeed, writes most plainly in the twelfth book of the Antiquities that Jason and Menelaus were brothers of Onias. Hence Lyra, in this place, rejects Josephus, on account of the authority of this book. But the Master in the Histories [Peter Comestor, in the *Historia scholastica*] and many other authentic and ancient Catholics have followed Josephus: and reasonably, as it seems. For the Jews would not have borne Menelaus in the high priesthood unless he had been of the race of Aaron. Nor after the return from the Babylonian captivity are the Jews ever read to have had any high priest except of the stock of Levi and Aaron. As for Menelaus being called the brother of the aforesaid Simon, some explain it by saying that he was his brother not by descent in the flesh, but by imitation of his malice and likeness to it; in which manner it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:27|He that sheddeth blood, and he that defraudeth the laborer of his hire, are brothers|Qui effundit sanguinem, et qui fraudem facit mercenario, fratres sunt]]. It could also be said that, since the tribe of Levi could join in marriage with the other tribes of Israel, this Menelaus was perhaps of the tribe of Benjamin on one parent's side, especially the mother's, and so Simon's brother.

paras.t: At ille, videlicet Menelaus, commendatus regi Antiocho ab ejus ministris, qui ad hoc faciendum erant (ut creditur) a Menelao per dona inducti, quum magnificasset faciem potestatis ejus, id est, regem et ejus potentiam magnifice commendasset, in semetipsum retorsit summum sacerdotium, id est, procuravit illud sibi a rege donari ambitiose, simoniace, fraudulenter. Acceptisque a rege mandatis quid ageret, et ut pro pontifice susciperetur, venit, etc. Et Jason, qui proprium fratrem captivaverat, id est, causa fuit quod Onias seorsum reclusit se, ut infra habetur, in Ammanitem, id est regionem Ammonitarum, expulsus est. Huc enim sacerdotii principatu privatus aufugit. De pecuniis vero regi promissis Menelaus nihil agebat, id est, eas Antiocho non persolvit, quum exactionem faceret, id est, persolvi eas regi exigeret, Sostratus, sicut et vectigalia persolvi exegit; qui Sostratus arci quæ fuit in monte Sion, præsidebat. Quam ob causam utrique, videlicet Menelaus et Sostratus, ad regem sunt evocati, ad reddendum rationem, cur Menelaus regi non solvit quod debuit. Et comperto quod Menelaus fuit in culpa, amotus est a sacerdotio, id est pontificatu, succedente Lysimacho fratre suo, qui de semine Aaron fuit, ut probabilius reputatur.
paras.en: [[4:24|But he|At ille]], namely Menelaus, [[4:24|being recommended to the king|commendatus regi]] Antiochus by his ministers, who had been induced to do this (as is believed) by Menelaus with gifts, [[4:24|when he had magnified the appearance of his power|quum magnificasset faciem potestatis ejus]], that is, had magnificently praised the king and his might, [[4:24|got the high priesthood for himself|in semetipsum retorsit summum sacerdotium]] [literally 'turned the high priesthood back upon himself'], that is, procured that it be given him by the king, ambitiously, simoniacally, fraudulently. [[4:25|So having received the king's mandate|Acceptisque a rege mandatis]] as to what he should do, and that he should be received as high priest, [[4:25|he returned|venit]], etc. [[4:26|Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother|Et Jason, qui proprium fratrem captivaverat]] [*captivaverat*, literally 'had taken captive'], that is, was the cause that Onias shut himself away apart, as is told below, [[4:26|was driven out|expulsus est]] [[4:26|into the country of the Ammonites|in Ammanitem]] (*Ammanites*, that is, the region of the Ammonites). For he fled there, deprived of the leadership of the priesthood. As for [[4:27|the money he had promised to the king|De pecuniis vero regi promissis]], Menelaus [[4:27|took no care|nihil agebat]], that is, did not pay it to Antiochus, when Sostratus [[4:27|called for it|quum exactionem faceret]], that is, required it to be paid to the king, as he also required the taxes to be paid; for this Sostratus was in charge of the castle that was on mount Sion. This is why [[4:28|they were both|utrique]], namely Menelaus and Sostratus, [[4:28|called before the king|ad regem sunt evocati]], to give account why Menelaus had not paid the king what he owed. And when it was found that Menelaus was at fault, he [[4:29|was removed from the priesthood|amotus est a sacerdotio]], that is, the high priesthood, [[4:29|Lysimachus, his brother, succeeding|succedente Lysimacho fratre suo]], who was of the seed of Aaron, as is more probably held.

paras.t: Et quum hæc agerentur, contigit Tharsenses et Mallotas, id est cives ab urbibus suis sic nuncupatos, seditionem movere contra regem suum Antiochum, a quo videbantur contempti, eo quod Antiochi regis concubinæ dono essent dati, id est ob hoc, quod Antiochus dedit eos pro munere suæ concubinæ, ut essent sub illius dominatione. Festinanter itaque rex venit sedare illos, ne et concubinam suam contristaret, aut subditos contra se acrius provocaret, relicto suffecto, id est substituto, uno ex comitibus, id est principibus seu sociis sui regiminis, Andronico in Antiochia, ex qua venit sedare præfatos. Ratus autem, id est existimans, Menelaus accepisse se tempus opportunum procurandi interfectionem Oniæ, rege absente, aurea quædam vasa de templo furatus (quod sacrilegium fuit) donavit Andronico, ut ejus sibi amicitiam procuraret, sicque per eum obtineret Oniam occidi.
paras.en: [[4:30|When these things were in doing, it fell out that they of Tharsus, and Mallos|Et quum hæc agerentur, contigit Tharsenses et Mallotas]], that is, citizens so named from their cities, [[4:30|raised a sedition|seditionem movere]] against their king Antiochus, by whom they seemed to be slighted, [[4:30|because they were given for a gift to Antiochus, the king's concubine|eo quod Antiochi regis concubinæ dono essent dati]] [Denis's text reads 'to the concubine of King Antiochus'; the Vulgate names her, Antiochis], that is, because Antiochus gave them as a present to his concubine, to be under her dominion. [[4:31|The king, therefore, went in all haste to appease them|Festinanter itaque rex venit sedare illos]] [the words of this lemma are damaged in the scan and are given as in the Vulgate], lest he should both grieve his concubine and provoke his subjects more sharply against himself, leaving, [[4:31|for his deputy|relicto suffecto]], that is, as his substitute, [[4:31|one of his nobles|uno ex comitibus]], that is, one of the princes or companions of his government, [[4:31|Andronicus|Andronico]], at Antioch, from which he came to quiet the aforesaid. [[4:32|Then Menelaus supposing|Ratus autem]], that is, thinking, [[4:32|that he had found a convenient time|Menelaus accepisse se tempus opportunum]] to bring about the slaying of Onias while the king was away, [[4:32|having stolen certain vessels of gold out of the temple|aurea quædam vasa de templo furatus]] (which was sacrilege), [[4:32|gave them to Andronicus|donavit Andronico]], to win his friendship for himself, and so through him to have Onias killed.

paras.t: Qui Andronicus quum venisset ad Oniam, et suasisset ei de asylo procedere, id est, de loco illo in quo tutus fuit, nec poterat lædi, descendere, statim eum peremit. Propter quod, id est ob tam immanissimam impietatem, indignati sunt Judæi et Græci in Antiochia exsistentes, atque regresso regi conquesti sunt: qui Deo instigante usque ad lacrimas condoluit interfecto; et Andronicum purpura exutum, veluti degradatum, fecit occidi.
paras.en: [[4:34|And he went to Onias|Qui Andronicus quum venisset ad Oniam]], and [[4:34|persuaded him to come forth out of the sanctuary|et suasisset ei de asylo procedere]], that is, to come down from that place in which he was safe and could not be harmed, [[4:34|and immediately slew him|statim eum peremit]]. [[4:35|For which cause|Propter quod]], that is, on account of so monstrous an impiety, the Jews and the Greeks living at Antioch were indignant, and complained to the king on his return: and he, at God's prompting, grieved even to tears for the slain man; and [[4:38|he commanded Andronicus to be stripped of his purple|et Andronicum purpura exutum]], as though degraded, and had him put to death.

paras.t: Multis autem sacrilegiis, id est rerum sacrarum abusionibus, a Lysimacho in templo commissis, et divulgata fama de tantis criminibus, congregata est multitudo Judæorum vitia Lysimachi abominantium, adversus Lysimachum, multo jam auro exportato de templo per Lysimachum, illud in usus proprios convertentem. Turbis autem insurgentibus contra Lysimachum, Lysimachus armatis fere tribus millibus qui erant de parte ipsius, iniquis manibus, id est adjutorio impiorum illorum, uti cœpit. Et multi quidem vulnerati de adjutoribus Lysimachi, quidam autem et prostrati, id est occisi, omnes vero residui de ejus exercitu, in fugam conversi sunt; ipsum etiam sacrilegum Lysimachum, circa ærarium, scilicet extra templum, interfecerunt.
paras.en: [[4:39|Now when many sacrileges|Multis autem sacrilegiis]], that is, abuses of sacred things, [[4:39|had been committed by Lysimachus in the temple|a Lysimacho in templo commissis]], [[4:39|and the rumour of it was spread abroad|et divulgata fama]] of such great crimes, [[4:39|the multitude gathered themselves together|congregata est multitudo]] of the Jews who abhorred the vices of Lysimachus, [[4:39|against Lysimachus|adversus Lysimachum]], [[4:39|a great quantity of gold being already carried away|multo jam auro exportato]] from the temple by Lysimachus, who was turning it to his own uses. [[4:40|Wherefore the multitude making an insurrection|Turbis autem insurgentibus]] against Lysimachus, [[4:40|Lysimachus armed about three thousand men|Lysimachus armatis fere tribus millibus]] who were of his party, [[4:40|and began to use violence|iniquis manibus]] [literally 'to use wicked hands'], that is, the help of those wicked men. [[4:42|And many of them were wounded|Et multi quidem vulnerati]] among the helpers of Lysimachus, [[4:42|and some struck down to the ground|quidam autem et prostrati]], that is, slain, [[4:42|but all|omnes vero]] the rest of his force [[4:42|were put to flight|in fugam conversi sunt]]; [[4:42|and as for the sacrilegious fellow himself|ipsum etiam sacrilegum]] Lysimachus, [[4:42|they slew him|interfecerunt]] [[4:42|beside the treasury|circa ærarium]], that is, outside the temple.

paras.t: De his ergo cœpit judicium adversus Menelaum agitari, id est, Judæi cœperunt Menelao hæc crimina et sacrilegia Lysimachi imputare, quia consilio Menelai facta fuerunt. Et quum venisset rex Tyrum, ad ipsum detulerunt negotium missi viri tres a senioribus Judæorum: qui tres accusaverunt Menelaum coram rege. Et quum superaretur Menelaus, id est, objectionibus et accusationibus contra se factis respondere non posset, promisit Ptolemæo, amico seu consiliario regis, multas pecunias ad suadendum regi, id est, ut persuaderet Antiocho Menelaum reum non esse, sed accusatores ipsius. Et ad sententiam deduxit, id est, Ptolemæus ille iniquus induxit regem ad proferendum sententiam pro Menelao. Miseros autem, id est accusatores Menelai miserabiliter criminatos et circumventos, qui etiam si apud Scythas, id est homines sic vocatos, qui crudeles irrationabilesque dicuntur, causam dixissent, id est, negotium contra Menelaum proposuissent, innocentes judicarentur a Scythis, quia apertissime justa fuit eorum causa; hos morte damnavit Antiochus.
paras.en: [[4:43|Now concerning these matters, an accusation was laid against Menelaus|De his ergo cœpit judicium adversus Menelaum agitari]], that is, the Jews began to impute to Menelaus these crimes and sacrileges of Lysimachus, because they had been done by Menelaus's counsel. [[4:44|And when the king was come to Tyre|Et quum venisset rex Tyrum]], [[4:44|three men were sent from the ancients to plead the cause before him|ad ipsum detulerunt negotium missi viri tres a senioribus]] of the Jews: and these three accused Menelaus before the king. [[4:45|But Menelaus being convicted|Et quum superaretur Menelaus]], that is, being unable to answer the objections and accusations made against him, [[4:45|promised Ptolemee|promisit Ptolemæo]], the king's friend or counsellor, [[4:45|much money to persuade the king|multas pecunias ad suadendum regi]], that is, to persuade Antiochus that not Menelaus was guilty, but his accusers. And he [[4:46|brought him to be of another mind|Et ad sententiam deduxit]] [Denis reads *ad sententiam*, 'brought him to a sentence', where the Vulgate has *a sententia*, 'from his opinion'], that is, that wicked Ptolemee brought the king to pronounce sentence for Menelaus. As for [[4:47|those poor men|Miseros autem]], that is, the accusers of Menelaus, pitiably charged and circumvented, who, even if [[4:47|before Scythians|apud Scythas]] (that is, men so called, who are said to be cruel and unreasoning) [[4:47|they had pleaded their cause|causam dixissent]], that is, had set out their case against Menelaus, [[4:47|should have been judged innocent|innocentes judicarentur]] by the Scythians, since their cause was most plainly just: these [[4:47|were condemned to death|hos morte damnavit]] by Antiochus.

paras.t: Cito ergo injustam pœnam dederunt, id est, passi sunt (juxta quem modum loquendi ait Apostolus: Qui pœnas dabunt in interitu æternas), qui pro civitate Jerusalem et populo Judæorum, et sacris vasis templi, causam prosecuti sunt contra Menelaum coram rege. Menelaus autem propter eorum qui in potentia erant avaritiam, id est propter cupiditatem principum Antiochi, quibus munera contulit Menelaus, permanebat in potestate, id est sacerdotii principatu.
paras.en: So they [[4:48|did soon suffer unjust punishment|Cito ergo injustam pœnam dederunt]] (*dederunt*, literally 'gave', that is, suffered; in which manner of speaking the Apostle says: [[2 Thess 1:9|Who shall suffer eternal punishment in destruction|Qui pœnas dabunt in interitu æternas]]), [[4:48|that persecuted the cause for the city, and for the people, and the sacred vessels|qui pro civitate Jerusalem et populo Judæorum, et sacris vasis templi, causam prosecuti sunt]] against Menelaus before the king. [[4:50|And so through the covetousness of them that were in power|Menelaus autem propter eorum qui in potentia erant avaritiam]], that is, through the greed of the princes of Antiochus, on whom Menelaus bestowed gifts, [[4:50|Menelaus continued in authority|permanebat in potestate]], that is, in the leadership of the priesthood.

paras.t: Ecce quanta fiunt in hoc mundo facinora, et qualiter justi ac pii ab impiis opprimuntur, ipsique impii prosperantur ad tempus, secundum dispensationem secretorum judiciorum Altissimi. Propter quod Isaias dicit: Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet in corde suo; et viri misericordiæ colliguntur, et non est qui intelligat. Quæ res interdum movet fideles in admirationem, juxta illud Habacuc primo: Quare, Domine, respicis contemptores, et taces, conculcante impio justiorem se? Propter hoc lacerata est lex, quia impius prævalet adversus justum. Propterea egreditur judicium perversum. Sed si respicimus ad futuri sæculi retributiones, atque ad ordinem infinitæ sapientiæ providentiæque Dei, admiratio cessat.
paras.en: Behold how great crimes are done in this world, and how the just and godly are oppressed by the wicked, and the wicked themselves prosper for a time, according to the dispensation of the secret judgments of the Most High. Wherefore Isaias says: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart, and men of mercy are taken away, because there is none that understandeth|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet in corde suo; et viri misericordiæ colliguntur, et non est qui intelligat]]. This thing sometimes moves the faithful to wonder, according to that of Habacuc, chapter one: [[Hab 1:13|Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|Quare, Domine, respicis contemptores, et taces, conculcante impio justiorem se?]] [Denis's wording, 'Why, O Lord, dost thou look upon the despisers … while the wicked treads down', differs a little from the Vulgate's] [[Hab 1:4|Therefore the law is torn in pieces|Propter hoc lacerata est lex]], [[Hab 1:4|because the wicked prevaileth against the just, therefore wrong judgment goeth forth|quia impius prævalet adversus justum. Propterea egreditur judicium perversum]]. But if we look to the rewards of the world to come, and to the order of the infinite wisdom and providence of God, the wonder ceases.
